transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I came in because... lately, I've been having to be more in front of people for my job—I help plan events and conventions. And ever since that started, I just can't stop staring at this one part of my face in photos. It looks really uneven to me. I keep looking at it, even though everyone else tells me they barely see anything at all. It's just really bothering me.
When you're not looking at photos or mirrors, do you still think about this part of your face throughout the day, or does it mainly bother you when you see your reflection?

Um, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really noticed. I mean, it definitely bothers me a lot when I see a picture or look in the mirror, but... I don't know if I'm constantly thinking about it when I'm just walking around or working. I haven't really paid attention to whether it stays on my mind when I'm not looking at it.

When you're at work or doing other activities during the day, do you find yourself thinking about this facial feature popping into your head on its own, even when you're not looking at a mirror or photo?

Um, like I was just saying, I really just don't know. I haven't noticed if it pops into my head on its own like that. When I'm at work, I'm usually pretty busy running around setting things up, so... yeah, I just can't say for sure if it's on my mind when I'm away from a mirror or a camera.
In the past week, have you caught yourself thinking about this facial feature at times when you weren't looking at a mirror or photo—like while you're working, eating, or talking to someone?

Honestly, it's exactly like I just said. I really don't know. I haven't been keeping track of my thoughts like that during the week. When I'm eating or talking to someone, I'm usually just focused on what I'm doing. So... yeah, I just can't give you a yes or no on that. I've only really noticed it being an issue when there's a mirror or a camera around.

Over the past few days, have you noticed yourself worrying about how this part of your face looks at times when you weren't looking in a mirror or at a photo—like while you're lying in bed at night, or during a quiet moment?

I feel like you keep asking me the same thing, just in different ways. And... I really just don't have a different answer for you. 

Even at night when I'm lying in bed, I haven't noticed if I'm worrying about it then. I usually just try to go to sleep. Like I've been saying, I only really notice it bothering me when I actually see my reflection or look at a picture. I just haven't paid attention to whether it's on my mind during those quiet moments.

When you do look at photos or in the mirror, do you find yourself spending a lot of time examining that part of your face, or do you sometimes ask friends or family members if they think something looks wrong with it?

Yeah, that is exactly when it happens. Like, before I send out event pictures or right before I join a vendor meeting, I'll just keep checking my face in my phone camera. 

I end up retaking photos over and over, or I try to tilt my head a certain way so it doesn't look as bad. And I do ask people sometimes—like I'll ask a coworker if I look weird. It actually takes up a lot of time... enough that I sometimes fall behind on my planning stuff because I'm stuck doing all that.

When you're checking your face in the mirror or retaking those photos, does it feel like something you choose to do, or does it feel more like something you have to do—like you can't stop yourself even if you wanted to?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I guess I just do it. I haven't really thought about whether I'm choosing to do it or if I can't stop. It's just... what happens when I see a camera or a mirror. I haven't really paid attention to whether it feels like a choice or not.

When you're NOT looking in a mirror or at a photo, and this thought about your face pops into your head on its own, can you easily push it away and stop thinking about it, or does it tend to stick around even when you try not to think about it?

Like I said before, I really only think about it when I'm looking at a mirror or a picture. So I don't really have those thoughts popping into my head when I'm not looking at my reflection. I just... I don't know if I could push them away or not, because it just doesn't happen that way for me.

Let me ask this differently: In a typical day, if you completely avoided mirrors and cameras—didn't look at any photos or reflections—would you still find yourself thinking about this facial feature on your own, or would it basically not be on your mind at all that day?

If I completely avoided mirrors and cameras? I think... well, I guess if I didn't see my reflection at all, it probably wouldn't be on my mind. I'm pretty busy with my event planning stuff, so if I'm not looking at a screen or a mirror, I'm usually just focused on my work. So yeah, I don't think I'd really think about it much if I didn't have to see it.

You mentioned that checking your face and retaking photos sometimes causes you to fall behind on your event planning work. Beyond just losing time, how much does this concern about your face bother you emotionally—would you say it causes you significant distress, or is it more of a minor annoyance?

I guess... I wouldn't say it's a minor annoyance, but I'm not sure if it's significant distress either. It definitely bothers me when I realize I've wasted a bunch of time and now I'm rushing to get my work done. That stresses me out. But the actual feeling about my face... it's just frustrating, you know? I get annoyed with how it looks in the picture or the mirror, and I just want to fix it so I can move on. So, it bothers me, yeah, but I don't know if I'd use the word distress.

Over the past week, have you had any moments where you suddenly thought about how that part of your face looks, without you intentionally bringing it to mind—like an unwanted thought that just popped up?

No, not really. Like I was saying earlier, it just doesn't really happen like that for me. Thinking about this past week... no, I haven't had any thoughts just pop up out of nowhere. If I'm not looking at a mirror or dealing with photos, my mind is just on my event planning or whatever else I'm doing. So, no, I haven't had any unwanted thoughts suddenly come up like that.

When you're in social situations at work—like talking with coworkers or clients face-to-face—does the thought about how that part of your face looks ever cross your mind during those interactions, even though you're not looking at a mirror or camera?

Um... no, not really. When I'm talking to clients or running an event, I'm just thinking about the event. I'm making sure everything is on schedule, talking to the caterers, that kind of thing. Since I'm not looking at a picture of myself or anything, it doesn't really cross my mind. I'm just focused on getting the job done.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with appearance-related concerns triggered by occupational demands (increased visibility in event planning role), but lacks the core diagnostic features of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD). Specifically: (1) intrusive, repetitive thoughts about the facial feature occur only when viewing mirrors/photos, not spontaneously throughout the day; (2) the patient denies unwanted intrusive thoughts; (3) functional impairment is present but limited to time spent on mirror-checking/photo retaking rather than pervasive avoidance; (4) distress level is described as frustration/annoyance rather than significant emotional distress. The symptom pattern is better characterized as an adjustment-related concern with some compulsive checking behaviors, meeting criteria for Unspecified Nonorganic Somatoform Disorder (F48.9). F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) was considered given the work-related stress trigger, but anxiety symptoms are not the primary presentation.

confirmed_symptoms: Repeated mirror checking and photo retaking
Seeking reassurance from coworkers about appearance
Attempts to conceal or minimize appearance concern through head positioning
Repetitive checking of face in mirror and phone camera
Multiple photo retakes before sending images
Behavioral avoidance/modification (tilting head to minimize appearance)
Acknowledged discrepancy between self-perception and others' observations
Lack of spontaneous intrusive thoughts when not viewing mirrors/photos
Thoughts limited to mirror/photo viewing situations

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Recent onset following occupational role change requiring increased visibility in front of people; specific duration not quantified but appears to be weeks to months.
additional_requirements: Functional impairment confirmed: time spent checking mirrors/retaking photos causes delays in event planning work
Psychosocial stressor confirmed: occupational demand increase (more visibility in event planning role)
Absence of core BDD criterion: no pervasive intrusive thoughts outside of mirror/photo viewing contexts
Mild to moderate distress level: patient describes frustration and annoyance rather than severe emotional distress
